trap: Becomes a jurisdictional argument about Peter and papal authority (missing the pastoral point), or a private orthodoxy quiz — missing that the confession is revealed to Peter, not achieved by him: he didn't reason his way there.
hinge: The mouth that just spoke the truest thing anyone in the Gospel has said will, six verses later, be called "Satan" for refusing the cross. The rock and the stumbling-block are the same man in the same conversation.

doors.landing: Whom do men say, whom do you say
doors.claim: The crowd's guesses — John, Elijah, a prophet — are all half-true and none of them enough; the question turns from public opinion to personal confession.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Beautifully is the question put, 'Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?' For they who speak of the Son of Man, are men.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: He says not, Whom do the Scribes and Pharisees say that I am? but, Whom do men say that I am? searching into the minds of the common people... and by a second question invites them to higher thoughts.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: He wills that their errors be set forth, so that, these being driven off, the disciples may bring forth the truth, not out of the opinion of the common people, but out of the Lord's revelation.

doors.say: Every crowd has an opinion about Jesus, and none of them are quite the truth — the question isn't settled until it's asked of you.
doors.do: Have them write down what "people say" about Jesus today, then set it aside and answer the question themselves.

doors.claim: Peter did not reason his way to the confession — flesh and blood did not reveal it, the Father did. The church's foundation is a gift received, not a conclusion argued.

witnesses.author: Hilary of Poitiers
witnesses.reading: This confession of Peter met a worthy reward, for that he had seen the Son of God in the man... to have looked and to have seen beyond human sight is matter of praise.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: It was on him, as on a rock, that the Church was built. But I know that since that I have often explained... that this rock was Christ.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Flesh and blood — that is, thy own reason, or any natural power whatsoever.

doors.say: Peter didn't figure this out — it was shown to him. What you know rightly about Jesus was given to you, not earned by you.
doors.do: Ask them to name one true thing about Jesus they now hold that they once could not have reasoned their way to.

doors.landing: Gates of hell, keys of heaven
doors.claim: The promise is not a grant of institutional power but authority over the real enemy — sin and the grave, opened by binding and loosing in Christ's name.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: Every spiritual sin is a gate of hell, to which are opposed the gates of righteousness.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: Let him then be without blame who binds or looses another, that he may be found worthy to bind or loose in heaven.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: The gates of hell are sins, threats, blandishments, heresies, by which the weak rush into death. He who receives the faith of Christ in the inmost love of the heart easily overcomes whatever assails.

doors.say: The keys were never about who's in charge — they're about what actually holds people captive, and what sets them free.
doors.do: Have them name a sin they've watched "bind" someone, and pray specifically for its loosing this week.

doors.landing: Look to the rock you were hewn from
doors.claim: Isaiah answers discouragement with memory: know what you were cut from, and whose you are.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Look — consider the state of Abraham and Sarah, from whom all of you sprang.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Look unto the rock: Christ. Of which, And the rock was Christ, out of which you are hewn, from Christ called Christians.

doors.say: Before you decide what you are, remember what you were cut from.
doors.do: Ask them to tell one story of the faith that formed them to someone younger this week.

doors.claim: Abraham was one man in a hopeless case when God called him, and that is the pattern God uses to raise a forlorn church.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Him alone — to follow me to an unknown land: him only of all his kindred. Increased — into a vast multitude, when his condition was desperate in the eye of reason. And therefore God can as easily raise his church when they are in the most forlorn condition.

doors.say: God started the whole people of God with one old man and a barren wife. Small and desperate is where God likes to begin.
doors.do: Invite them to stop apologizing for being few, and to name one thing a small church can do this month that a large one cannot.

complementary.gravity: Isaiah tells discouraged exiles to look to the rock they were hewn from, to Abraham called alone and made many, and promises to make Zion's wilderness like Eden (Isaiah 51); the Psalm trusts the Lord to perfect what concerns us; Paul calls a body of many members to be transformed rather than conformed (Romans 12); and Jesus names Peter the rock on which he will build his church. The nerve: the church stands on what God has quarried and built, not on what it can make of itself.

synthesis.convergence: Isaiah sends the discouraged back to the rock they were cut from, and to one man God made into a people (Isaiah 51); the Psalm is sure the Lord will perfect what concerns us (Psalm 138); Paul sees many members with different gifts in one body (Romans 12); and Jesus builds his church on a confession Peter did not invent (Matthew 16). Each reading grounds God's people in God's own work of quarrying, calling, and building.
synthesis.claim: You were cut from a rock God chose and are built on a rock God laid; the church's future rests there, not on its own strength.
synthesis.here: For a congregation measuring itself by decline — fewer, older, smaller — the move is Isaiah's: look back at Abraham, called alone and made many, and trust the builder over the count.

semicontinuous.gravity: Pharaoh's decree to kill every Hebrew boy is undone by two midwives who fear God more than the king (Exodus 1-2); the Psalm sings of a soul escaped like a bird from the snare; Paul urges "be transformed by the renewing of your mind," not conformed to the age (Romans 12); and Jesus asks the question that decides everything: "Who do you say that I am?" The nerve: the answer that saves comes not from majority opinion but from a mind renewed enough to see past the crowd's guesses.

synthesis.convergence: Two midwives defy an empire's decree out of fear of God, not fear of Pharaoh (Exodus 1); Paul insists the renewed mind stops being conformed to its age (Romans 12); Peter's confession only lands because he has stopped repeating what "men" say and heard what the Father reveals. Every text asks whose voice actually governs you — the empire's, the crowd's, or the one revealed from above.
synthesis.claim: The crowd's opinion of Jesus is not nothing, but it will never be enough — until you say who he is for yourself.
synthesis.here: For a congregation absorbing every hot take about Jesus from the culture around them, the move is Peter's: stop reciting what everyone else says, and answer the question put to you directly.

subtract: Three landings — from crowd-opinion to confession, the gift of revelation, or the real stakes of the keys. Choose one. A fourth door — Peter as rock of papal authority — is deliberately not opened here: it's ecumenically loaded, and Augustine's own later clarification (above) already complicates a simple reading. Raise it only if directly asked.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
